parole.significato: The edible and aromatic seed pods (properly, capsules) of the Abelmoschus moschatus.
parole.testo: From New Latin abelmoschus, from Arabic حَبّ الْمِسْك (ḥabb al-misk, “pills of musk”).

parole.significato: Any of the various tropical flowering plants of the genus Abutilon, such as the flowering maple, Indian mallow, or Chin…
parole.testo: From New Latin [Term?], from Arabic أَبُو طِيلُون (ʔabū ṭīlūn, “Indian mallow”).

parole.significato: Ethiopian; Eritrean; Abyssinian.
parole.testo: From Renaissance Latin Abyssīnī (“the Abyssinians”), from Arabic الْحَبَشَة (al-ḥabaša), from حَبَش (ḥabaš, “Abyssinian”). The humorous use of Abyssinia as a parting phrase is due to its phonetic resemblance to I'll be seeing ya.

parole.significato: The "salt of wisdom" of the alchemists, a double salt composed of the chlorides of ammonium and mercury, formerly used…
parole.testo: From post-classical Latin alembrottus, likely derived from an Arabic term; further etymology uncertain.

parole.significato: Elementary algebra: A system for representing and manipulating unknown quantities (variables) in equations.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin algebra, from the Arabic الْجَبْر (al-jabr, “reunion, resetting of broken parts”) in the title of al-Khwarizmi's influential work الْكِتَاب الْمُخْتَصَر فِي حِسَاب الْجَبْر وَالْمُقَابَلَة (al-kitāb al-muḵtaṣar fī ḥisāb al-jabr wa-l-muqābala, “The Compendious Book on Cal

parole.significato: A universal solvent sought by the alchemists.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Late Latin alcahest, apparently coined by Paracelsus as a pseudo-Arabism.

parole.significato: A pear-shaped pot with an opening at each end, formerly used, especially by alchemists, for sublimation.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin aludel, from Arabic الأُثَال (al-ʔuṯāl, “the sublimation vessel”).

parole.significato: An alloy containing mercury.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin amalgama (“mercury alloy”), from Arabic اَلْمَلْغَم (al-malḡam, “emollient poultice or unguent for sores”), from Ancient Greek μάλαγμα (málagma, “emollient; malleable material”), from μαλάσσω (malássō, “to soften”), from μαλακός (malakós, “soft”). Doublet of malagma. For the verb

parole.significato: A chemical element (symbol Sb, from Latin stibium) with an atomic number of 51: in its stable allotrope, a lustrous gra…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin antimonium, attested in the 11th century; see also the Wikipedia section.

parole.significato: A tree, Adansonia digitata, native to tropical Africa, having a broad swollen trunk and edible gourd-like hanging fruit…
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin bahobab, from Arabic أَبُو حِبَاب (ʔabū ḥibāb, “father of many seeds”), from أَبُو (ʔabū, “father”) + حَبّ (ḥabb, “seed”).

parole.significato: Any of the thorny shrubs of genus Berberis, which bear yellow flowers and red or blue-black berries.
parole.testo: From Middle English berberie, from Medieval Latin berberis (on which see Arabic بَرْبَارِيس (barbārīs)), influenced by berie (“berry”). Doublet of berberis and related to Berber.

parole.significato: Any of various plants imported into Europe for the pharmaceutical trade in dried form, so of uncertain identity.
parole.testo: A Medieval Latin transcription of the Arabic بَهْمَن (bahman).

parole.significato: Relating to, or impregnated with borax.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin borax (genitive boracis), itself via Arabic بَوْرَق (bawraq), from Persian بوره (bura).

parole.significato: A biennial plant of species Carum carvi, native to Europe and Asia, mainly grown for its seed to be used as a culinary…
parole.testo: From Middle English caraway, carewey, carwey, from Medieval Latin carui, from Arabic كَرَاوِيَا (karāwiyā), via Aramaic from Ancient Greek καρώ (karṓ), κάρον (káron, “caraway”).

parole.significato: The branch of natural science that deals with the composition and constitution of substances and the changes that they…
parole.testo: First coined 1605, from chemist + -ry. From chemist, chymist, from Latin alchimista, from Arabic اَلْكِيمِيَاء (al-kīmiyāʔ), from article اَل (al-) + Ancient Greek χυμεία (khumeía, “art of alloying metals”), from χύμα (khúma, “fluid”), from χυμός (khumós, “juice”), from χέω (khéō, “to pour”).

parole.significato: Relating to or using chemicals or chemistry.
parole.testo: Back-formation from compounds built on New Latin chēmicus (“pertaining to alchemy or chemistry”) and chēmia (“chemistry”), ultimately of Ancient Greek origin.

parole.significato: To treat a material with a boiling liquid and repeatedly return the distillate.
parole.testo: From New Latin cohobātus, past participle of cohobāre, perhaps from Arabic كَعَّبَ (kaʕʕaba).

parole.significato: The tough and inflexible outermost of the three layers of the meninges, enveloping the brain and spinal cord.
parole.testo: First attested c. 1400, borrowing from Medieval Latin dūra māter (literally “firm, strict mother”), ellipsis of dūra māter cerebrī (literally “hard mother of the brain”), calque of Arabic أُمّ الدِّمَاغ الصَفِيقَة (ʔumm al-ddimāḡ aṣ-ṣafīqa, literally “thick mother of the brain”).

parole.significato: A liquid which converts lead to gold.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin elixir (“philosopher's stone”), from Arabic اَلْإِكْسِير (al-ʔiksīr, “philosopher's stone”), from Ancient Greek ξηρίον (xēríon, “powder for drying wounds”), from ξηρός (xērós, “dry”).

parole.significato: The fruit of Emblica officinalis (now Phyllanthus emblica, the Indian gooseberry, once used as a remedy against dysente…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin emblicus, from Arabic أَمْلَج (ʔamlaj), from Sanskrit आमलक (āmalaka). Doublet of amla.

parole.significato: A mineral of metamorphosed limestones. Lazurite forms the gemstone lapis lazuli, and crushed lazurite provided the ultr…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin lazur (“lapis lazuli”) (from Arabic لَازَوَرْد (lāzaward), from Persian لاژورد (lâžvard)) + -ite.

parole.significato: A medicine in a soft form taken by licking; a lambative, a linctus.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin lohoc, looch, from Arabic لَعْق (laʕq, “to lick”).

parole.significato: An ornamental shrub, Daphne mezereum, having purple flowers and bright red fruit.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mezereon, mezereum, from Arabic مَازَرْيُون (māzaryūn).

parole.significato: The abdominal wall.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin mirac, mirach, from Arabic مَرَقّ (maraqq, “delicate and sensible part of the venter”), from رَقَّ (raqqa, “to be soft”).

parole.significato: The point of the celestial sphere, directly opposite the zenith; inferior pole of the horizon; point of the celestial s…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nadir, from Arabic نَظِير السَّمْت (naẓīr as-samt), composed of نَظِير (naẓīr, “counterpart, corresponding to”) and السَّمْت (as-samt, “the zenith”).

parole.significato: A water lily, especially the European white water lily (Nymphaea alba) or the yellow water lily (Nuphar lutea).
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin nenuphar, from Arabic نِلُوفَر (nilūfar), نِينُوفَر (nīnūfar), from Middle Persian nylw(k)pl (nīlōpal, “lotus, water-lily”), from Sanskrit नीलोत्पल (nīlotpala, “blue lotus”), from नील (nīla, “blue”) + उत्पल (utpala, “lotus, water-lily”). Compare French nénufar.

parole.significato: Of or pertaining to the back or nape of the neck.
parole.testo: Borrowed from Medieval Latin nuchālis, from nucha + -ālis, from Arabic نُخَاع (nuḵāʕ, “spinal cord”).

parole.significato: The outermost celestial sphere of the heavens in Ptolemaic astronomy, which was believed to cause all the inner spheres…
parole.testo: From Middle English primum mobile (“outermost celestial sphere causing other spheres to move”), borrowed from Medieval Latin prīmum mōbile (literally “first mover”), a calque of Arabic مُحَرِّك أَوَّل (muḥarrik ʔawwal, “first mover”), which is itself a calque of Ancient Greek τὸ πρῶτον κινῆσαν (tò p

parole.significato: The wrinkling and creases on the inner surface of the wrist.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rasceta, rasca, rascha, rasga, misread from Arabic رُسْغ (rusḡ).

parole.significato: A mineral, arsenic sulfide (AsS), often associated with orpiment and stibnite in lead, silver and gold ores.
parole.testo: From Middle English realgar, from Medieval Latin realgar, resalgar, from Arabic رَهْج اَلْغَار (rahj al-ḡār, literally “cave dust”).

parole.significato: A syrup made of evaporating fruit juice over a fire, usually mixed with sugar or honey, and especially used for medicin…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin rob, from Arabic ربّ (“thickened fruit juice”). Compare French rob, Spanish rob, Italian rob, robbo, Portuguese robe, arrobe, Persian ربودن (present stem: robâ).

parole.significato: The dorsal vein of the little finger, bleeding from which was anciently held to be a treatment for melancholy.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin salvatella, misread from salacella, misread from salaseilem, misread from alaseilem, from Arabic الْأُسَيْلِم (al-ʔusaylim).

parole.significato: A prominent vein or nerve, the saphenous vein
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin saphena, from Arabic صَافِن (ṣāfin), from Hebrew צֹפֵן (ṣōfēn, “hiding”).

parole.significato: Concave or cup-shaped.
parole.testo: From Latin scyphātus, erroneously interpreted as scyphus (“cup, goblet”) + -ātus; in reality, probably derives from Arabic شَفَة (šafa, “edge, rim”), and refers to the distinctive and conspicuous border of the early histamena gold coins.

parole.significato: A medium-sized deciduous tree of species Cordia myxa or, less often, Cordia latifolia, Cordia sebestena, or other speci…
parole.testo: Learned borrowing from Medieval Latin sebesten, from Arabic سِبِسْتَان (sibistān), from Persian سگپستان (sag-pestân, literally “dog teat”), from سگ (sag, “dog”) + پستان (pestân, “teat”).

parole.significato: Abnormal, especially excessively deep, sleep.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin subeth (adjective: subethicus), from Arabic سُبَات (subāt, “ailment of excessive sleep”)

parole.significato: An irrational number, especially one expressed using the √ symbol.
parole.testo: First attested in the mid 16th century from Latin surdus (“deaf, mute”), used in mathematics for “irrational,” reflecting ἄλογος (álogos, “irrational, speechless”) as found in Euclid, apparently transmitted via Arabic جِذْر أَصَمّ (jiḏr ʔaṣamm, “deaf root”). The phonetic sense, “voiceless,” emerged

parole.significato: Powdered and perfumed talc for toilet use.
parole.testo: From talc + -um, from Medieval Latin talcum, from Arabic طَلْق (ṭalq).

parole.significato: Operculina turpethum (obs. syn. Convolvulus turpethum, Ipomea turpethum, Merremia turpethum), a plant in the morning gl…
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin turpethum, from Arabic تُرْبِد (turbid), from Persian تربد (torbed), from Sanskrit त्रिपुटा (tripuṭā), त्रिपुट (tripuṭa), literally “triplicated”, names of several plants.

parole.significato: Curcuma zedoaria, a perennial herb native to India and Indonesia.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin zedoārium, from Arabic جَدْوَار (jadwār), from Classical Persian ژدوار (žadwār).

parole.significato: The point in the sky vertically above a given position or observer; the point in the celestial sphere opposite the nadi…
parole.testo: From Middle English cenyth, from Medieval Latin cenit, from Arabic سَمْت (samt, “direction, path”), from the fuller form سَمْت اَلرَّأْس (samt ar-raʔs, “direction of the head”). The -ni- for -m- is sometimes thought to be due to a misreading of the three strokes, which is plausible, though it could

parole.significato: Zingiber zerumbet, a Javanese plant resembling ginger.
parole.testo: From Medieval Latin zerumbet, zurumbet, from Arabic زُرُنْبَاد (zurunbād).
